newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia charges Soros foundation with tax evasion.
newsitem.headline: Croatia charges Soros foundation with tax evasion.

text.p: Croatia's financial police on Monday charged the local branch of an international humanitarian foundation sponsored by U.S. billionaire George Soros with financial malpractice and tax evasion.

State radio said a police investigation at the Zagreb headquarters of the Soros-sponsored Open Society had found evidence of "illegal financial transactions". The charges were forwarded to the state prosecutor, the radio said.

The move came after weeks of anti-Soros campaigning that began when President Franjo Tudjman branded Soros an "enemy of the state" at the annual congress of his nationalist ruling HDZ party last month.

A police statement released on Monday alleged Soros employees had been receiving double salaries since December last year -- a regular one in Croatian currency (kuna) and another in U.S. dollars, which was not reported for state tax.
In his speech, Tudjman said the foundation had "infiltrated" all of Croatian society, and accused it of trying to change the ownership structure of cultural and media institutions.

The Croatian leader accused Soros and "other American and European foundations" of supporting the Croatian opposition by helping small magazines and systematically enlarging the scope of their activities.
Shortly after Tudjman's speech, police confiscated $65,000 from two foundation members at the Croatian border. The two were released after questioning but the money was not returned.
On top of Monday's charges, the police said further fines might be imposed on the society for violating the law on hard currency transactions.
"This is the beginning of the implementation of Tudjman's speech. It will paralyse the foundation," an official from the organisation told Reuters.
The Soros Foundation finances several media and cultural projects to promote democracy in Eastern Europe, and has donated more than $15 million in various forms since 1993.
It was banned briefly in neighbouring rump Yugoslavia.
